steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on SMiLE, a schema-augmented multi-level contrastive learning framework for knowledge graph link prediction. Motivate link prediction, review the existing method families, explain why entity context and schema matter, and finish with our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Knowledge graphs, incompleteness and link prediction
2. Existing link prediction methods
3. Limitation: entity context and diverse entity representations
4. Key challenge and why schema helps
5. Our schema-augmented multi-level contrastive learning framework
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. KGs and link prediction
- KG = well-structured representation of knowledge; vast human knowledge as triples (head, relation, tail)
- used in AI applications: question answering, recommendation systems
- real-world KGs incomplete: many valid links missing
- link prediction: predict whether relation exists between head and tail entity -> triple construction and verification

2. Existing methods
- rule-based: Markov logic networks; reinforcement learning-based method -> learn logic rules from KG
- KG embeddings: translational (TransE, TransR); semantic matching (RESCAL, DistMult)
- embedding methods + graph neural networks for graph topology; type information to enhance representations

3. Limitations
- fail to model contextual information in entity neighbors
- context keeps structural + semantic info; link prediction depends on contexts of entities/triples
- diversity of entity representations across contexts ignored -> false predictions
- FB15k: 14579 entities, 154916 triples, 14417 entities with types (98.89%); 13853 (95.02%) more than two types; 10.02 types per entity on average
- Figure 1: Nicole Kidman, types Actress and Citizen
  - upper left: "Awards and works of Nicole Kidman as an actress" -> relation to 66 th Cannes fine
  - (Nicole Kidman, ?, Lane Cove Public School) makes no sense from Actress (no Actress-School relation)
  - but she is also an Australian citizen -> prediction reasonable

4. Key challenge / schema
- challenge: encapsulate complex contexts of entity neighborhoods
- whole subgraph as context -> redundant, noisy info
- schema = high-order meta pattern of KG, type constraint between entities and relations -> captures structural + semantic info in context
- inconsistent representations: need diverse representations per context; schemas define different type restrictions -> subtle, precise semantics
- same schema -> similar features; different contexts -> disparate

5. Our framework
- inspired by contrastive learning: schema-augmented multi-level contrastive learning framework for link prediction
- schema incomplete -> extract/build <head_type, relation, tail_type> tensor from input KG
- multi-level contrastive learning guided by schema; contextual-level and global-level objectives optimized separately
- contextual-level: contrast entities in subgraphs of same schema
- global-level: cross-view contrast between contexts of an entity
- pre-train entity representations, then fine-tune entities and relations

6. Contributions (three)
- multi-level contrastive learning framework, contextual info in entity embeddings; different representations from different contexts
- hard negative sampling with KG schema as prior constraint; contrast at contextual- and global-level
- experiments on four kinds of KG datasets; outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on link prediction

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A knowledge graph (KG) is a well-structured way of representing knowledge, and it stores a huge amount of human knowledge as triples (head, relation, tail). KGs are important parts of many artificial intelligence applications, for example question answering and recommendation systems. But in the real world KGs are always incomplete, which means that a lot of valid links are missing from the KG. So link prediction techniques, which try to automatically predict if a relationship exists between a head entity and a tail entity, are essential for building and verifying triples.

Many methods have been proposed for link prediction in KG. Traditional rule-based methods such as Markov logic networks and a reinforcement learning-based method learn logic rules from the KG and use them to do link prediction. The other main group of methods is based on knowledge graph embeddings. These include translational models like TransE and TransR and semantic matching models like RESCAL and DistMult. Also, embedding-based methods use graph neural networks to explore the graph topology and use type information to make the representations in KG better.

However, these methods do not model the contextual information in the neighbors of an entity. The context of an entity keeps specific structural and semantic information, and the link prediction task basically depends on the contexts of specific entities and triples. Also, not much attention is paid to the fact that an entity can have diverse representations in different contexts, and this can often lead to wrong predictions. To give some numbers, the dataset FB15k has 14579 entities and 154916 triples, and 14417 entities (98.89%) have types. 13853 entities (95.02%) have more than two types, and each entity has 10.02 types on average. For example, in Figure 1 the entity Nicole Kidman has two different types (Actress and Citizen), and these express different semantics in two different contexts. The upper left part of the figure describes contextual information at the type level about "Awards and works of Nicole Kidman as an actress". Here it makes sense that there is a relation between Nicole Kidman and 66 th Cannes, and intuitively predicting (Nicole Kidman, ?, Lane Cove Public School) does not make sense, because there is no direct relationship between type Actress and type School. But Nicole Kidman is also an Australian citizen, so it is reasonable to make this prediction.

4. Key challenge / schema
- challenge: encapsulate complex contexts of entity neighborhoods
- whole subgraph as context -> redundant, noisy info
- schema = high-order meta pattern of KG, type constraint between entities and relations -> captures structural + semantic info in context
- inconsistent representations: need diverse representations per context; schemas define different type restrictions -> subtle, precise semantics
- same schema -> similar features; different contexts -> disparate

5. Our framework
- inspired by contrastive learning: schema-augmented multi-level contrastive learning framework for link prediction
- schema incomplete -> extract/build <head_type, relation, tail_type> tensor from input KG
- multi-level contrastive learning guided by schema; contextual-level and global-level objectives optimized separately
- contextual-level: contrast entities in subgraphs of same schema
- global-level: cross-view contrast between contexts of an entity
- pre-train entity representations, then fine-tune entities and relations

6. Contributions (three)
- multi-level contrastive learning framework, contextual info in entity embeddings; different representations from different contexts
- hard negative sampling with KG schema as prior constraint; contrast at contextual- and global-level
- experiments on four kinds of KG datasets; outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on link prediction

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A knowledge graph (KG) is a well-structured way of representing knowledge, and it stores a huge amount of human knowledge as triples (head, relation, tail). KGs are important parts of many artificial intelligence applications, for example question answering and recommendation systems. But in the real world KGs are always incomplete, which means that a lot of valid links are missing from the KG. So link prediction techniques, which try to automatically predict if a relationship exists between a head entity and a tail entity, are essential for building and verifying triples.

Many methods have been proposed for link prediction in KG. Traditional rule-based methods such as Markov logic networks and a reinforcement learning-based method learn logic rules from the KG and use them to do link prediction. The other main group of methods is based on knowledge graph embeddings. These include translational models like TransE and TransR and semantic matching models like RESCAL and DistMult. Also, embedding-based methods use graph neural networks to explore the graph topology and use type information to make the representations in KG better.

However, these methods do not model the contextual information in the neighbors of an entity. The context of an entity keeps specific structural and semantic information, and the link prediction task basically depends on the contexts of specific entities and triples. Also, not much attention is paid to the fact that an entity can have diverse representations in different contexts, and this can often lead to wrong predictions. To give some numbers, the dataset FB15k has 14579 entities and 154916 triples, and 14417 entities (98.89%) have types. 13853 entities (95.02%) have more than two types, and each entity has 10.02 types on average. For example, in Figure 1 the entity Nicole Kidman has two different types (Actress and Citizen), and these express different semantics in two different contexts. The upper left part of the figure describes contextual information at the type level about "Awards and works of Nicole Kidman as an actress". Here it makes sense that there is a relation between Nicole Kidman and 66 th Cannes, and intuitively predicting (Nicole Kidman, ?, Lane Cove Public School) does not make sense, because there is no direct relationship between type Actress and type School. But Nicole Kidman is also an Australian citizen, so it is reasonable to make this prediction.

We think that the key challenge in keeping contextual information in embeddings is how to encapsulate the complex contexts of entity neighborhoods. If we just take all the information in the subgraph of an entity as the context, we may bring in redundant and noisy information. Schema is a high-order meta pattern of KG and it contains the type constraint between entities and relations, so it can naturally be used to capture the structural and semantic information in the context. For the problem of inconsistent entity representations, we have to consider the diverse representations of an entity in different contexts. Different schemas define different type restrictions between entities, so schema can keep subtle and precise semantic information in a specific context. Also, to get consistent and robust entity representations for each contextual semantics, entities in contexts of the same schema should have similar features, and they should be different in different contexts.

To solve these issues, and inspired by advanced contrastive learning techniques, we propose a new schema-augmented multi-level contrastive learning framework for efficient link prediction in KGs. Because the KG schema is also incomplete, we first extract and build a <head_type, relation, tail_type> tensor from the input KG to represent the high-order schema information. Then we design a multi-level contrastive learning method that is guided by the schema. We optimize the contrastive learning objective at the contextual-level and at the global-level of our model separately. At the contextual-level, contrasting entities in subgraphs of the same schema learns semantic and structural characteristics in a specific context. At the global-level, a cross-view contrast captures the differences and global connections between the contexts of an entity. Overall, we use this contrastive strategy to get entity representations with structural and high-order semantic information in the pre-train phase, and then we fine-tune the representations of entities and relations to learn subtler knowledge of KG.

Our three main contributions are the following:

- We propose a new multi-level contrastive learning framework that keeps contextual information in entity embeddings. We also learn different entity representations from different contexts.

- We design a new way to sample hard negatives using the KG schema as a prior constraint, and we do the contrast estimation at both the contextual-level and the global-level, which makes the embeddings of entities in the same context closer and pushes apart entities in dissimilar contexts.

- We run extensive experiments on four different kinds of knowledge graph datasets and show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on the link prediction task.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Knowledge graph (KG), as a well-structured representation of knowledge, stores a vast amount of human knowledge in the format of triples (head, relation, tail). KGs are essential components for various artificial intelligence applications, including question answering [1], recommendation systems [2], etc. In the real world, KGs always suffer from the incompleteness problem, meaning that a large number of valid links in KG are missing. In this situation, link prediction techniques, which aim to automatically predict whether a relationship exists between a head entity and a tail entity, are essential for triple construction and verification.

To address the link prediction problem in KG, a variety of methods have been proposed. Traditional rule-based methods like Markov logic networks [3] and reinforcement learning-based method [4] learn logic rules from KGs to conduct link prediction. The other mainstream methods are based on knowledge graph embeddings, including translational models like TransE [5], TransR [6] and semantic matching models like RESCAL [7], DistMult [8]. Besides, embedding-based methods use graph neural networks to explore graph topology [9] and use type information [10] to enhance representations in KG.

Nevertheless, these methods fail to model the contextual information in entity neighbors. In fact, the context of an entity preserves specific structural and semantic information, and the link prediction task essentially depends on the contexts related to specific entities and triples. Furthermore, little attention is paid to the diversity of entity representations in different contexts, which may often result in false predictions. Quantitatively, dataset FB15k has 14579 entities and 154916 triples, and the number of entities with types is 14417 (98.89%). There are 13853 entities (95.02%) that have more than two types, and each entity has 10.02 types on average. For example, entity Nicole Kidman in Figure 1 has two different types (Actress and Citizen), expressing different semantics in two different contexts. The upper left of the figure describes the contextual information at type level about "Awards and works of Nicole Kidman as an actress". In this case, it is well-founded that there is a relation between Nicole Kidman and 66 th Cannes, while intuitively the prediction of (Nicole Kidman, ?, Lane Cove Public School) does not make sense, since there is no direct relationship between type Actress and type School. But considering that Nicole Kidman is also an Australian citizen, it is reasonable to conduct such a prediction.

We argue that the key challenge of preserving contextual information in embeddings is how to encapsulate complex contexts of entity neighborhoods. Simply considering all information in the subgraph of entities as the context may bring in redundant and noisy information. Schema, as a high-order meta pattern of KG, contains the type constraint between entities and relations, and can naturally be used to capture the structural and semantic information in context. As for the problem of inconsistent entity representations, the diverse representations of an entity need to be considered in different contexts. As different schemas define diverse type restrictions between entities, schema is able to preserve subtle and precise semantic information in a specific context. Additionally, to yield consistent and robust entity representations for each contextual semantics, entities in contexts of the same schema should contain similar features but be disparate in different contexts.

To tackle these issues, inspired by advanced contrastive learning techniques, we propose a novel schema-augmented multi-level contrastive learning framework to allow efficient link prediction in KGs. To tackle the incompleteness problem of KG schema, we first extract and build a <head_type, relation, tail_type> tensor from an input KG [11] to represent the high-order schema information. Then, we design a multi-level contrastive learning method under the guidance of schema. Specifically, we optimize the contrastive learning objective at the contextual-level and global-level of our model separately. At the contextual-level, contrasting entities within subgraphs of the same schema learns semantic and structural characteristics in a specific context. At the global-level, differences and global connections between contexts of an entity are captured via a cross-view contrast. Overall, we use this contrastive strategy to obtain entity representations with structural and high-order semantic information in the pre-train phase, and then fine-tune representations of entities and relations to learn subtler knowledge of KG.

To summarize, we make three major contributions in this work:

- We propose a novel multi-level contrastive learning framework to preserve contextual information in entity embeddings. Furthermore, we learn different entity representations from different contexts.

- We design a novel approach to sample hard negatives using KG schema as a prior constraint, and perform the contrast estimation at both contextual-level and global-level, pulling the embeddings of entities in the same context closer while pushing apart entities in dissimilar contexts.

- We conduct extensive experiments on four different kinds of knowledge graph datasets and show that our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on the link prediction task.
